title: Crystal Palace Dinosaurs
summary: This document is about the Crystal Palace Dinosaurs, a series of world-first dinosaur and extinct animal sculptures in Crystal Palace Park, South London, commissioned in 1852 and unveiled in 1854. It begins with an overview explaining that the sculptures were designed by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins under the scientific direction of Sir Richard Owen, represent 15 genera of extinct animals (only three of which are true dinosaurs), and are notable for reflecting the inaccuracies of early paleontology, having received Grade II listed status in 1973, extensive restoration, and Grade I listed status in 2007. The History section traces the project from the relocation of the Crystal Palace after the Great Exhibition, Hawkins' construction methods, the display of models on three islands arranged as a geological timeline, the famous 1853 New Year's Eve dinner inside an Iguanodon mould, the funding cuts of 1855, Hawkins' later work in New York, the gradual decline and disrepair of the models, and successive restoration efforts through 1952, 2001–2002, the 2021 installation of a swinging bridge to Dinosaur Island, and a 2021 emergency renovation of the Megalosaurus sculpture. The Dinosaur Park section provides detailed descriptions of the models organized by geological era—Palaeozoic (Dicynodon), Mesozoic (Hylaeosaurus, Ichthyosaurus, Iguanodon, Labyrinthodon, Megalosaurus, Mosasaurus, Plesiosaurus, Pterodactylus, and Teleosaurus), and Cenozoic (Anoplotherium, Megaloceros, Megatherium, and Palaeotherium)—highlighting the scientific misconceptions embodied in each model and their subsequent condition and treatment. A final section on cultural impact covers the sculptures' appearances in literature by authors such as H. G. Wells, E. Nesbit, Dorothy L. Sayers, Paul Theroux, and Penelope Lively, as well as engravings, documentaries, and Historic England's 2023 creation of 3D photogrammetric models. The document concludes with references, sources, further reading, and external links, including resources from the Friends of Crystal Palace Dinosaurs charity.
